items.title: Mark Cuban says Meta knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads generating $16 billion in fraud-linked revenue, internal documents reveal [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
items.summary:
Mark Cuban accused Meta of knowingly allowing AI-generated deepfake scam ads on Facebook that target vulnerable users, including older adults, resulting in significant financial losses. Internal Meta documents revealed the company expected about $16 billion in revenue from ads linked to scams and prohibited products in 2024, with users seeing around 15 billion high-risk ads daily.

Meta's internal safety staff estimated its platforms contribute to a third of successful scams in the U.S., with automated systems only banning advertisers when there is a 95% likelihood of fraud. Meta disputed the documents' portrayal, citing a 58% drop in scam ad complaints and removal of over 134 million scam ads in 2025. Older Americans reported losing $7.7 billion to internet crimes in 2025, with AI-related scams accounting for over $352 million in losses among reported cases.

Cuban urged caution when encountering ads featuring famous faces and recommended verifying products for scams, especially to protect older family members. The FBI encourages reporting suspected scams promptly to aid in recovery efforts, though many victims do not file complaints.

items.title: Researcher expresses skepticism about the ingenuity of current autonomous AI R&D based on observed limitations in side projects and model performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
items.summary:
A researcher shared doubts about the perceived ingenuity of autonomous AI research and development after monitoring several side projects, including building a Scrabble engine, an Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe bot, and AI philosophy research. They observed that AI models often showed poor judgment, such as failing to identify key literature, conducting uninformative experiments, and pursuing trivial directions in complex tasks.

The researcher noted that improvements often came from human guidance and steering rather than the models' autonomous innovation. They highlighted challenges like models producing difficult-to-understand reports and the need for iterative prompting to achieve better results. This skepticism contrasts with some hill-climbing tasks where AI showed more effective progress under directed effort.

items.title: Thinking Machines launches Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with vision input and improved agentic coding, available on Tinker with weights to be open-sourced after safety review [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Inkling 2 Small
items.summary:
Thinking Machines introduced Inkling 2 Small, its second-generation AI model featuring 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active parameters, supporting image inputs and variable effort. The model surpasses previous versions in coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning, achieving a score of 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Initially available through the Tinker platform with closed weights, the full model weights are planned for release under an Apache 2.0 license following external safety testing and red-teaming.

Inkling 2 Small was trained with reinforcement learning on extensive long-horizon coding and autoresearch tasks, improving instruction following, verification, and usability in agent loops. It incorporates a 292M-parameter vision encoder enabling strong visual capabilities such as OCR and visual reasoning, and it demonstrated superior performance in tasks like wine identification from images. The model supports fine-tuning and sampling on Tinker, with downloadable checkpoints to be provided alongside the open weights release.

items.title: Nasdaq falls 5.5% for worst day in 19 months as investors anticipate AI regulation after Democratic election wins [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Nasdaq worst day in 19 months, investors bet on AI slowdown after Democrats win
items.summary:
The Nasdaq composite index dropped 5.5%, marking its worst day in 19 months and entering correction territory with over $2 trillion wiped off its value. The decline followed Democratic victories in US midterm elections, which raised investor concerns about potential regulatory restrictions on AI datacenter expansions and technology sector growth.

Chip stocks led the sell-off, with companies like SanDisk and Western Digital falling sharply, while the VIX volatility index surged 61%. The downturn extended to Asian markets, reflecting global investor anxiety about the future pace of AI development amid expected political hurdles. Analysts noted that Democratic control could slow datacenter buildouts and increase legislative challenges for AI and tech industries in the coming years.

items.title: Google donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to CNCF to support scalable, secure AI agent orchestration [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Google Donates Agent Substrate and GVisor to the CNCF
items.summary:
Google has contributed its Agent Substrate and gVisor projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) to foster community collaboration and development within the cloud native ecosystem. Agent Substrate is designed to efficiently manage AI agents by separating stateful actors from compute workers, addressing challenges like idle resource waste and control plane overload that traditional Kubernetes cannot handle.

Agent Substrate enables AI agents to maintain state while minimizing resource use during idle periods and supports rapid wake-up times under 500 milliseconds. Google announced this donation at KubeCon North America 2026, marking these projects as Sandbox-level CNCF initiatives aimed at advancing secure, scalable AI agent infrastructure.

items.summary:

The study found that while Claude is less used for idea generation and data gathering, specialized AI tools could increase its role in these areas.

The report suggests that widespread adoption of current AI capabilities could double research output in some fields, with potential increases up to 15-fold in computer science and statistics if AI handles all non-physical research tasks. Researchers surveyed expect AI models to conduct full research projects independently by 2030, indicating significant future impacts on the pace of scientific discovery.

Clutch was last valued at $85 million in early 2025 and is approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue, indicating a valuation of roughly 50 times ARR if the deal completes.

items.title: InfoQ Architecture & Design: Enterprise IAM requires identity as a core architectural element beyond authentication, emphasizing data models, access relationships, and revocation policies
items.originalTitle: Article: Identity as an Architectural Concern: Enterprise IAM Beyond Authentication
items.summary:
The article argues that identity management must be integrated into enterprise architecture rather than treated as an afterthought, especially in regulated environments where auditability of access is critical. It highlights that traditional role-based access control (RBAC) models fall short when managing complex relationships like ownership and validity of service accounts, advocating for graph-based models to better represent these connections.

Drawing from experience in financial services, the article discusses how designing identity as part of the data model enables precise queries about access history and ownership, which are essential for compliance audits. It also covers practical governance challenges such as managing service account owners during personnel changes and reducing revocation latency by merging attestation, rotation, and vaulting workflows into a unified process.

The piece underscores that identity design decisions impact service boundaries and event flows, requiring architectural consideration to ensure security and compliance at scale. It advises organizations to record every access grant and revocation as timestamped events to facilitate audit queries and maintain consistent security postures across distributed systems.

items.originalTitle: We are building an AI design tool that skips the prompt
items.summary:
Grafista is building an AI graphic design tool that removes the need for text prompts, aiming to help users without design or prompt engineering skills create professional-looking designs. The tool replaces traditional chatbot interfaces with visual inputs to guide the AI, addressing challenges users face with prompt-based design tools that often produce repetitive or mediocre results.

The company argues that while chatbots have simplified user interfaces, they require users to learn effective prompting, which can be difficult and time-consuming, especially for complex tasks like graphic design. By focusing on visual references instead of text commands, Grafista aims to streamline the design process and produce more unique, high-quality outputs without requiring advanced skills.

items.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Small (17A-594B), trained on 12 trillion tokens in 68 hours, outperforming Muse Spark [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: [AINews] Inkling 2 Small: 17A-594B trained in 68 hours on 12T tokens, beating Muse Spark
items.summary:
Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Small, a 594 billion parameter multimodal mixture-of-experts model trained from scratch on 12 trillion tokens over 68 hours. The model supports text and image input with text output and features a 1 million token context window. It is currently available on the Tinker platform, with Apache 2.0 open weights expected after external safety testing.

Inkling 2 Small is noted for its competitive performance against similar-sized Chinese models and Western counterparts like Mistral and Meta Muse. The training utilized native NVFP4 precision and included a reinforcement learning phase. The model emphasizes customizability and fine-tuning efficiency, positioning it as a leading open-weight model developed outside China according to current rankings.

items.title: Linum.ai releases Pyramid-JiT text-to-image model trained for $21K with Apache 2.0 licensed weights [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
items.summary:
Linum.ai, a two-person research lab, has released the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT) text-to-image model trained for approximately $21,000, offering an experimental open-source model under the Apache 2.0 license. The model uses a novel architecture that compresses image tokens more aggressively than typical approaches, enabling faster training and inference with fewer samples compared to previous versions.

The P-JiT model operates in pixel space and integrates a frozen Qwen3.5-4B text encoder with a diffusion-based image generator, achieving a 32×32 token reduction that significantly lowers computational costs. This release serves as a proof of concept toward Linum.ai's broader goal of developing efficient generative video models that democratize animation creation by making inference faster and cheaper.

items.title: Google open-sources Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin to scale design-driven AI software development with context-rich and stateless AI sessions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Elephant-Goldfish Model: scaling design-driven AI development
items.summary:
Google has released the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin as open source under the Apache 2.0 license to support design-driven AI software development. The framework uses "Elephant" sessions for long-term architectural design and "Goldfish" sessions for stateless validation, aiming to improve code reliability by aligning human system comprehension with AI execution.

The plugin automates the development lifecycle by managing context transfer between design and validation phases, guiding developers through brainstorming, drafting detailed design documents, and adversarial review by multiple AI instances. Thousands of Google engineers use this tool internally to ship production code, and the open-source release includes customizable workflows and integration support for various development environments.

This approach addresses the risks of increased coding speed without sufficient guardrails by emphasizing structured design and validation, potentially reducing bugs and improving software quality in AI-assisted development workflows.

items.originalTitle: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, an update to its video generation model that supports native 15-second clips, multi-turn conversational editing, and enhanced adherence to visual references. The new version reduces costs by 30% compared to its predecessor and is available through the Gemini API and Google Cloud for professional video production.

The update allows users to create longer videos with precise control over duration and improved consistency in characters, objects, and scenes across frames. It also enables faster editing through conversational prompts without needing to regenerate entire clips. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash supports clearer lip-sync and more natural multi-speaker dialogue, making it suitable for creating branded ads, virtual try-ons, and social media content at scale.

items.title: Tinyfish.ai shares lessons from building a deep research system that iteratively searches, browses, and synthesizes web data into long-form reports with citations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Lessons from Building a Deep Research System
items.summary:
Tinyfish.ai developed a deep research system designed to investigate topics by searching the web, browsing sites, gathering evidence from multiple sources, and producing detailed reports with citations. The project revealed that challenges centered more on context management, orchestration, and product design than on research itself. The system architecture includes an orchestrator that plans and executes research by invoking tools like search and browsing, continuously refining understanding and generating partial reports for users.

Initially, the system separated planning and execution into distinct components, but this caused issues with maintaining context across iterative research cycles. The orchestrator accumulated understanding over time, while the planner operated with limited context, leading to inconsistencies in follow-up queries. To address this, planning was integrated into the orchestrator's reasoning loop, preserving context and improving coherence. The experience highlights the costs of information boundaries in multi-component AI systems and the importance of unified reasoning processes for reliable agent design.

items.title: Obelisk Club reports 9.8% of top-charting App Store apps mention AI, with 26.7% of free apps offering in-app purchases or subscriptions as of November 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: App Store 2026 in numbers: AI, pricing, abandoned apps
items.summary:
Obelisk Club analyzed 178,637 apps appearing in the App Store top charts across 173 countries since October 2026, finding that nearly 10% mention AI-related terms and over a quarter of free apps monetize through in-app purchases or subscriptions. The study also revealed that 20.3% of these apps have not been updated for a year or more, and subscription pricing is the most common complaint in low-rated reviews.

The report highlights that AI mentions are concentrated in Graphics & Design, Photo & Video, and Developer Tools categories, with apps selling in-app purchases or subscriptions being three times more likely to mention AI. Independent developers account for 67.3% of charting apps, maintaining similar ratings to larger publishers. The research will be updated quarterly to track trends such as AI adoption and app maintenance over time.

items.summary:
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky has started a new AI lab and sold some intellectual property to this venture for $7.1 million in cash, as disclosed during Airbnb's third-quarter earnings report. The company also secured rights to invest in future equity financings of the lab and to license certain intellectual property for internal use.

Airbnb's Chief Technology Officer Ahmad Al-Dahle holds equity in the AI lab and, like Chesky, provides services to the venture. This move reflects a growing trend of tech CEOs pursuing side projects alongside their primary executive roles.

items.originalSummary:
Once upon a time, being CEO of a public company was a full-time job. In fact, for most CEOs, it still is—and an exhausting one at that. So it’s a little puzzling to see that a growing number of tech CEOs are embarking on their own side quests, including most recently Airbnb’s Brian Chesky, who has started an AI lab, as Bloomberg reported earlier this year.

Airbnb disclosed Thursday, as it reported third-quarter earnings, that it had sold some intellectual property to Chesky’s new venture for $7.1 million in cash. Airbnb also got the right to invest in any future equity financings of the venture and to license “certain” IP of the lab for internal use in Airbnb’s business. (Hopefully, the IP Airbnb will license isn’t the same IP it just sold to the lab.) Get this: It’s not just Chesky who is involved. Airbnb Chief Technology Officer Ahmad Al-Dahle also has equity in the venture and, like Chesky, “performs services” for it.

items.summary:

The company will limit confidentiality to legitimate security, trade secrets, or proprietary information and will establish local compacts reflecting community priorities for each new data center it operates.

In addition to dropping NDAs, OpenAI pledged to cover the full electricity costs and infrastructure for its data centers, publish expected job creation figures, and report on hiring to support local communities. This move follows similar steps by Amazon and aims to increase transparency and address concerns about data center developments.

items.originalTitle: Can Cheaper AI Outrun the Data Center Backlash?
items.summary:
US election results have led to increased restrictions on data center expansion, raising concerns among tech executives and investors about higher costs for running AI workloads. Despite rising prices for Nvidia hardware and server rentals, AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic report significant efficiency improvements in their models, reducing per-task costs and potentially offsetting infrastructure constraints.

Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman expressed optimism about continuing data center growth despite local resistance and project cancellations. However, investors showed mixed reactions, favoring established cloud providers over smaller ones awaiting approvals. The impact of regulatory backlash is expected to be more pronounced for data centers planned for 2028 and beyond, while AI firms with high profit margins may have room to lower prices to sustain demand.

items.originalSummary:
After U.S. voters on Tuesday elected officials who are pushing to restrict data center expansion, some tech executives and investors are concerned that new delays in standing up computing capacity will make existing servers for AI more expensive to run.

And if computing becomes even pricier, there’s a question of whether declines in the cost of running AI could slow down.

So far this year, the cost of running AI has been falling, even as the price of renting servers has risen. For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, released in late September, can perform comparably to a bigger OpenAI flagship model, GPT-6 Astra, when used with a high reasoning setting. Yet the newer model costs about a fifth as much on a per-task basis as the older model, research firm Artificial Analysis said.

Anthropic has touted similar efficiencies with its latest models. And that’s happening despite the fact that buying or renting Nvidia hardware has gotten a lot costlier this year.

As AI costs become a major concern at enterprises, the price-drop trend will need to persist or else customers might pull back.

One senior executive of a private equity firm that owns and develops data centers told me this week that they believe prices of AI models will keep falling due to “token efficiencies”—the ability of AI to do more work with less compute—thanks to both hardware and software advancements.

In other words, they said, such efficiencies would help offset constraints on data center expansion. Of course, the executive is heavily incentivized to say such things, given the financial bets their company has already made.

On Wednesday, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said during an event hosted by private equity firm Blackstone that he is optimistic about the company’s data center expansion despite the election results. “We feel like we're in a pretty good spot, and I think others may have some more work to do.”

To be sure, Amazon has faced significant local resistance to some of its data center projects, and even had to drop a project in Virginia this year.

Garman didn’t comment on whether he expects server rental prices to rise further. But stock investors seemed to think so initially, based on the way they bid up shares of major cloud providers Wednesday while selling off stocks of smaller cloud providers that still need approvals for new facilities. (The major cloud providers pared back some of the gains during a selloff Thursday.)

Notably, many facilities that are supposed to come online next year have gotten some or all of the necessary state or local approvals, so the effects of the electoral backlash might have a big impact on facilities aiming to launch in 2028 and beyond.

Anthropic’s initial public offering prospectus offers another signal that the price of using its models has room to fall: the company’s gross profit margins have hovered around 85% in the first nine months of the year. (That excludes the cost of developing the models themselves.) So it may have some slack to lower prices if it needs to boost demand.

items.summary:
Perplexity has introduced Teammates, its own version of always-on AI agents designed for workplace use, competing with OpenAI's Dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet. These agents can handle multiple roles simultaneously within a workspace, leveraging existing projects, skills, and memory from Perplexity's tools.

Teammates work alongside Perplexity Computer, an AI system that deploys agents on user devices to complete tasks, but they extend capabilities by enabling collaboration on ongoing, large-scale work. Users can monitor Teammates' progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app and interact with them via Slack. Access to Teammates requires a subscription to Perplexity's $200 per month Max plan.

items.originalTitle: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
items.summary:
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said the Democratic wins in the recent midterm elections could make it harder for companies to build data centers, as political opposition and community pushback against these projects increase. She linked the backlash to broader public concerns about AI technology and emphasized the need for the industry to better communicate the benefits of data centers and AI.

Meta has operated data centers in 23 states and plans several large projects, but Powell McCormick noted that future developments will face more scrutiny and require clear local benefits, such as supporting local labor and funding public services. Despite these challenges, Meta expects its investments in AI and data center compute capacity to remain valuable, with demand for leasing compute resources continuing to grow.

items.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Cyber model for vulnerability hunting, finds hundreds of Linux and Firefox security issues amid rising AI-driven cyber threats [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough?
items.summary:
OpenAI has released a new cybersecurity-focused AI model, ChatGPT Cyber, available to top-tier users in its Daybreak Red program for offensive security research. The model has already identified 948 potential vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel and 81 novel issues in Firefox, highlighting AI's growing role in both discovering and potentially exploiting software flaws.

Security researchers using OpenAI's earlier GPT 5.6 Sol model found a severe Ubuntu server vulnerability, demonstrating how AI can rapidly uncover complex bugs that humans might miss. OpenAI is investing $1 billion to support cybersecurity professionals working on critical infrastructure, but experts warn that the pace of AI-driven vulnerability discovery may outstrip defenders' resources, especially as some AI tools are being restricted to limit misuse.

While OpenAI dedicates significant compute power to pro bono vulnerability research, the scale of investment remains modest compared to other AI projects. The company emphasizes a narrow window for defenders to patch critical systems before AI capabilities become more accessible to malicious actors, underscoring the urgent need for expanded security efforts in the AI era.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI president Greg Brockman says company could be IPO ready in 2027
items.summary:
OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company could be ready for an initial public offering in 2027, citing strong growth in its enterprise revenue. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference, Brockman highlighted how OpenAI has gained ground in the enterprise market, where competitors like Anthropic had previously established a presence.

Brockman noted that OpenAI's enterprise business has doubled and now accounts for the majority of its revenue, up from about 30% previously. He attributed the growth to sustained investments and partnerships with clients such as JPMorgan Chase. The company has shifted from being perceived mainly as a consumer-focused firm to a committed enterprise AI provider, emphasizing building trust and delivering measurable milestones for business customers.

items.summary:
Scott Wiener, the California politician who led the successful effort to pass AI safety legislation in the state’s legislature last year, is headed to Washington. The state senator won Tuesday’s election to succeed long-time House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, after his opponent conceded on Wednesday. 

When Wiener arrives in D.C., he will be among the few members of Congress to have authored significant AI legislation. Last year, Calif. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Wiener’s SB 53, which requires the largest AI companies to write and comply with their own safety policies for managing severe risks from their technology.

The bill and the AI companies that supported it could indicate the kind of AI policies that a Democrat-controlled Congress will get behind.

items.title: Voters’ Gift to Big Tech [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Voters’ Gift to Big Tech
items.summary:
Voters just handed big tech a gift—and we’re not just thinking of Californians who voted against the billionaire tax proposal. (Can all those billionaires come home now?) Wednesday’s rally in the stocks of Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet suggests that investors see lots of upside for those tech firms from Tuesday’s Democratic victory.

The vote put a lot of people into office who are no fans of AI and data centers. By implication, any slowdown in AI data center development will disproportionately hurt neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius—which haven’t built out their facilities as much as bigger and older cloud firms. Notably, both their stocks dropped sharply Wednesday. On the theory that anything that hurts your rivals is good for you, that’s good for big cloud firms Amazon, Microsoft and Google.

This ads stack has achieved significant commercial success with over $1 billion annualized revenue and 100,000 advertisers, demonstrating production readiness and operational maturity.
